D: In lonely solitude my home,
And from my cabin when I stray,
Where'er my wan'ring eyes may roam,
The landscape that doth round me lay,
How desolate, how drear
Doth it at autumn-e'en appear.
M: From my humble home gone forth,
P: The prospect from my cottage shows

And murmuring sounds my ear please,

The sweeping gusts of autumn pass.
N: The Autumn gusts pass, calling on
M: From the rice leaves at my gate

And would that I could catch
Its message, as it whistles through

D: Thy beauty is throughout the land
As well-known as the furious play
Of billow on Takashi's strand,
That drench the venturesome with spray,
Who come their sweep too nigh:
So she who hath thee once beheld,
To tears of jealous love compelled,
Her sleeve shall ne'er be dry.
N: Of the Takashi strand do drench
M: Of the fickle waves that beat
Should I e'er go near that shore
I should only wet my sleeves.
P: The sound of ripples on the shore
My sleeves all worn and wet with tears

D: The Sakura trees in plenty grow
On Takasago's steep hill-side,
And now their crowded blossoms show;
O may no fogs their beauty hide,
No mists from hill-top rise
To veil their radiance from our eyes.
N: The mists from the other hills
M: O'er the slope below the peak,
May the mists of hither hills
Not arise to veil the scene.
P: Oh may no mountain mist arise,
No clouds so soft and white,
To hide them from our sight.

D: As windy blasts down Hasse's steep
In furious path impetuous sweep,
So rudely thou my suit dost slight,
And scorn thy lover's hapless plight;
No more 'fore Hasse's shrine
Will I in suing prayer incline.
N: Nay, his heartlessness, to be furious?
M: As the storms of Hase's hills.
P: Oh! Kwannon, Patron of this hill,
The maid, for whom I pine,
What of those prayers of mine?

D: A covenant thou mad'st with me,
And as the Sasemo from th' dew,
So I my very life from thee
Drink in. Alas! I fear me
This autumn's days are now but few!
N: The sasaemo's life is a dew
M: Yet, alas! the year has passed

D: In fisher's barque I onward glide
O'er th' broad expanse of ocean's tide,
And towards th' horizons when I turn
My glance I scarcely can discern
Where the white-tipped billows end,
That with the cloud-horizon blend.
N: Over the expanse of sea I row.
M: As I row and look around,
That the white waves, far away,
P: When rowing on the open sea,
The waves, all capped with white,
Roll onward, like the fleecy clouds

D: The brawling strem against the rock
Its tumbling waters fiercely hurls,
Divided by the furious shock,
In double torret onwards whirls:
In further flow
I trow a single stream 'twill show.
N: Like a hurrying, rock-hurling mountain stream
I wish to be: its double torrents
M: By a rock met and restrained
P: The rock divides the stream in two,
And both with might and main
But well I know the twain

D: 'Tween Awaji and Suma fly
The screaming sea-birds to and fro
Night after night; their ceaseless cry
Doth scarce a moment's sleep allow,
To whom his fate
Allots the ward of Suma's gate.
N: By the cry of the plovers
How many nights art thou awakened,
M: From your sleep, how many nights
P: The birds scream in their flight
Full oft they've made the Suma Guard

D: When bloweth autumn's chilly blast,
Through rifts at times the moonbeams peep,
From 'mid the dark clouds drifting past,
And earth in pallid radiance steep,
I love to see
The bright-edged shadows o'er the lea.
N: From the rifts of the clouds
Drifting abroad in the Autumn wind,
P: See how the wind of autumn drives
The clouds to left and right,
While in between the moon peeps out,

D: I fear me thou wilt break the pact
Thou mad'st with me--thy love will pass
Away from me, whom thought distract,
As tangled as the unkempt mass
My raven tresses show,
That o'er my waking pillow flow.
N: To last long. Ah, this tangle
of the black tresses of mine!
Ah, my anxiety of this morn!
M: That he wills our love should last?
And this morn my anxious thoughts,
Like my black hair, are confused.
P: Tangled this morning are my thoughts,
As is my long black hair.

D: I heard the Hototogis cry,
I searched throughout the echoing sky,
No Hototogis could espy,
The morning moon but met my eye.
N: The sky where the cuckoo sung!
M: Toward the place whence I had heard
Was the moon of early dawn.
P: And lo! the branch is bare
I only see the morning moon,

D: What wretchedness is mine, O Life!
With what deep mis'ry thou'rt opprest!
With my sad lot I strive in strife
That leaveth me nor peace nor rest;
The tears that flow
Down o'er my cheek my anguish show.
N: And I have my life still
M: But my tears I can not keep;
They can not my grief endure.
P: How sad and gloomy is the world,
This world of sin and woe!
Ah! while I drift along Life's stream,

D: O'er th' world doth evil aye hold sway
I deemed, and far I fled away
Amis the hills:
But there the deer's sad cry, too, thrills.
N: Even into the deep of a hill
M: Way of flight I find nowhere.
Yet e'en there the stag's cry sounds.
P: From pain and sorrow all around
To mountain wilds should I retreat,

D: Were I to linger more in life,
What seemed of old a grievous strife
Would seem to be a burden slight,
To be borne almost with delight.
N: Were I to linger longer in life,
The present days would grow dear again:
The days I deemed sad in past.
M: Just as past time fraught with grief
Now comes fondly back in thought.
P: Time was when I despised my youth,
What would I give for boyhood now,

D: With wretched thoughts distracted I

I waited for the breaking day
Through chink of screen
That guards my chamber--peeping, seen.
N: All the night long I thought
Even the chink of my chamber door
Is heartless to me, not inviting the morn
P: In vain I look to try and see

D: With deeper melancholy sways

How down my cheek the tears roll.
N: The moon has nothing to make
But, alas, my own tears alone
M: That has made me sad, as though
P: O'ercome with pity for this world,
I wonder, can it be the moon

D: The passing shower onwards sweeps,--

The rising mist up yon hill-side
Of autumn e'en
At twilight's chilly hour seen.
N: The dews of the passing shower
Toward the maki leaves, this Autumn eve!
M: See the deep vale's mists arise
That still hold the dripping wet
P: The rain, which fell from passing showers,
Like drops of dew, still lies

N: Like a joint of the shore reed.)
Why do I long, exhausting me so?
M: Short as is a node of reed
Must I, henceforth, long for him
With my whole heart, till life's close?
P: I've seen thee but a few short hours;
As short, they seemed to me,
Can't gauge my love for thee.

D: Of my life or soon or late the thread,
The withering threat perforce must snap:
I almost would 'twere now, I dread
Of longer life the sure hap--
The secret of our love displayed,
For e'er our happiness low laid.
N: Be torn off now if it must!
My secret would be hard to keep.
M: If thou art to end, break now.
All I do to hide ( my love)
May at last grow weak (and fail).
P: Though I should try to hide,
Some day the thread will break, the pearls

D: I would that I might show to thee
The island-fisher's oft-drenched sleeve,
I would that thine own eyes might see
How the salt waves their tints ne'er thieve;
From mine, alas!
Aye tear-bedewed, the colours pass.
N: How the Oshima island fishers’ sleeves
Never change their tints, though wet through.
But, alas, tearful sleeves of mine!
M: Though wet through and wet again,
Do not change their dyer's hues.
P: The fisher's clothes, though cheap, withstand
But see I my floods of tears have blurred
As for thy love I grieve.

D: Now grasshopper's chirp the livelong night
I hear, now hoard-frost doth the ground
O'ercarpet, and in saddened plight,
My day-worn raiment yet unbound,
I strive in vain
On lonely couch reposo to gain.
N: Upon the mat of the frost night,
I, my raiment not yet unbound.
M: While all through the frosty night
P: I'm sleeping all alone, and hear
So cold and frosty is the night,

D: My sleeve is as the rook unseen,
Ne'er bared at lowest ebb of tide,
And none do guess my grief, I ween,
Now how my tear-drenched sleeve's ne'er dried.
N: Even at the lowest tide. Nobody would know
M: E'en at ebb-tide hid from view,
P: My sleeve is wet with floods of tears
As here I sit and cry;
Can find a spot that 's dry!

D: O that throughout an endless life
I might in peace dwell, far from strive!
For ever watch the fishing yawl,
And view the nets abundant haul:
How fair to me,
How pleasant such a lot would be!
N: Oh, to be carried away by the sight
Of a fisherman’s yawl at the shore,
And by his hauling of the net.
M: Might be ever as it is!
P: I love to watch the fishing-boats
The crew, all straining at the oars,

D: Now autumn-gusts sweep
Down Miyoshino's steep,
And far into the night so drear
The sound of beating of the cloth,
Borne to me on the night-wind forth,
From my lonely village home, I hear.
N: Down Miyoshino the Autumn wind blows,
From my mountain home is cold.
M: Sounds of beating cloth I hear.
P: This night so cold and clear.

D: An ignorant man am I, unfit
O'er all the multitude of men
In dignity supreme to sit:
The simple priest's black robe again
I would, a humble dweller on
Wagatasoma, gladly don.
N: Ah, to save the sad world,
M: I have dared to shield the folk
I, who live on Mount Hiei.
P: Unfit to rule this wicked world
With all its pomp and pride,
I'd rather in my plain black robe

D: The court with Sakura's flowers is strewn
As thick as though the drifted snow
Did thereon lay: and I too soon
As withered low shall lie 'neath blow
Of man's inevitable foe.
N: Is nothing but my own self.
M: Is it that here, withering, falls:--
That in truth is I, myself.
P: This snow is not from blossoms white
That whiten all my garden paths

D: On Matsu'ho's shore, our meeting place,
At dusky hour of night, I wait
My longed-for mistress to embrace;
Ah, why then linger'st thou so late!
My ardent passion, than the fire
That heats the salt-pans, rages higher.
N: Like fire heats the salt water
In the evening calm of Matsuho shore!
M: Waiting one who does not come.
P: For thee I pine and sigh;
Though calm and cool the evening air,
Are not more parched than I!

D: O'er Nara's streamlet softly blow
The winds in the now dim twilight,
the Misogi, thereby set, show
That summer hath not yet gone quite.
N: On the nara tree stream. To see
The Misogi feast might be the sign
M: Not a sign of summer left
P: The twilight dim, the gentle breeze
The splash of worshippers who wash

D: Some men me love, some men me hate
Inspire: whene'er I think upon
This miserable world, my gate
My pitiable doth seem to me.
M: Some men are hateful to me;--
To me, weighted down with care,
P: How I regret my fallen friends
And, tired of life, I only seek
To reach my long day's close,

D: On th' hundred-chambered palace lo
A rent and tattered roof is seen,
Where rank Shinobu weeds do grow:--
How long, how hard out pain hath been!
N: On the olden eaves! Oh, what longing
M: When I think of former days,
More than e'en the clinging vines
P: And o'er the roof the creeping vine

3.あしびきの: precedes 山鳥 (mountain bird) / 山 (mountain) words

4.白妙の: precedes 富士の高嶺 (snow-covered peak, white things)

8.うぢ: Meaning a place in Kyoto and gloomy.
8.山と: Old name for Japan and mountain.

17.千早ぶる: precedes 神代 (kamiyo, age of the gods)

75.をき: おく is a kake-kotoba meaning ‘do in advance’ or ‘rise’.

84.しのば: Shinoba is kakekotoba for 'endure' and 'think fondly'.

91.さむしろ: むしろ (‘straw mat’), さむし (‘cold’), and むし (‘insect’)

95.墨染: Meaning black dyed, and newly inhabited

N.arm: One part of kakekotoba, the other being "useless".

P.deer: The deer is mentioned in the poem, but not as hunted.

D.s'ye's pine-crown'd steep: 末の松山波こさじとは
